: Is there a technical beginning and ending to a master phase, officiall, I
: mean?
: For example, if during my master phase I am supposed to transfer 1 blood
: to some vampire of mine, do I necessarily have to do it BEFORE I play the

: still consider it the master phase, as long as it's before the next phase?

You can do things in whatever order you want. Your Master phase basically
lasts from the end of your untap phase until just before your first minion
action.

Well, the investments do require the Meth.'s personal attention
and care (expand a Master card-play), but since Blood Dolls
don't, I can't see why a Meth. can't Sudden Reversal and Blood
Doll, yet can take profit from an investment, create a new
Powerbase, /and/ suck on a Blood Doll.

Similar (kinda) with Chantry - the blood can come from any vampire.

I doubt that the issue about Out-of-Turn Masters was the consideration
when they decided on these `Master Phase effects'. The rules
nowhere mentioned Master Phase effects, and the wording in the
OOT Master rules make it seem likely that /none/ was intended
(except for proper substitutes for a Master card-play, i.e.
investments). If I were the rules editor and `Master Phase
effects' were intended, I would have mentioned that explicitly
in the OOT Master rules (`... and can't use any Master Phase
effects on your next turn').

Also, this may create a small balance problem with these two
rather powerful cards, by allowing them to be used on the
turn that they are played.

Blood Dolls working during the untap phase will make them even more more
powerful. Why? Well, Hunting Grounds work during the untap phase as well. As of
the current rules, you can't put more blood on a vamp than it's capacity,
therefore a Blood Dolled vamp will always have less than it's full capacity if
you take blood off it. If the Blood Doll is used in the untap phase however,
the blood could (theoretically) be taken off BEFORE the Hunting Grounds give
the vamps blood. I believe the designers have reasons behind these rules.

Yes, BUT...

The two clans which can play AoR are Gangrel and Nosferatu. Let us
assume for the sake of argument that you are playing primarily a Gangrel
deck. Gangrel have: Animalism (get AoR in play, two extra untapping
cards over anything else), Protean (agg damage, among other things) and
Fortitude.

The main problem with gangrel is that they are _really_ weak on bleeding
- their clan hoser reduces this even further. They are strong enough in
other areas, however, that people still play them for their combat
abilities.

Make AoR cumulative, and you have solved Gangrel's only glaring
weakness. Now they are free to put into play as many AoR as they can and
then just sit back and untap (using animalism/WWEF) while waiting for
their prey (or others) to get desparate enough to try and burn the AoR.
Intercept the attempt (using Raven spies/sports bikes) and rip through
the hapless vampire in combat using Fortitude and Protean to their best
effect.

The Gangrel need not even _worry_ about their 'clan hoser' anymore, as
enough AoR will now do the job for them. They don't have to go looking
for fights, as the fights will come to them and the opponents will soon
be in torpor. Lastly (and best of all), once you have 3-5 AoR in play
and oust your prey, they _stay in play_ and bleed the heck outta your
former grandprey, and so on down the line!

As you can see, I am perfectly content with AoR as it is. Seems balanced
to me...

combat + Presence Bleeds). Gangrel intercept can't catch real Stealth,
and Gangrel combat is vulnerable against Fortitute and long-range
Tremeres. Gangrels putting an AoR horde in play using Protean
untaps (or equivalent) may be a problem, but that is a problem
of untap cards in general, not of AoR.

Let's see ... your vampires can't intercept the AoR's + Protean
stealth, can't stealth through Animalism intercept, and
are "hapless" in combat against Gangrel which are using
AoR's and intercept, aside from combat. No intercept, no
stealth, and no combat. What does your deck do, at all?

>The Gangrel need not even _worry_ about their 'clan hoser' anymore, as

is not too hard to be burnt if you can put only 1 or 2 out.

>They don't have to go looking

>be in torpor. Lastly (and best of all), once you have 3-5 AoR in play
>and oust your prey, they _stay in play_ and bleed the heck outta your
>former grandprey, and so on down the line!

If the grandprey just sits there and wait for the Rats to come and get him,
he deserves to be ousted. Anybody can (D) burn the Rats, especially
the grandprey with a predator who is already busy with the rats.
Unlike bleeds, which can strike suddenly and hit you for 4 pool,
AoR's have to sit on the table one turn before they takes
effect.

AoR torporize opponents which have neither stealth nor combat.
In other words, opponents which can never present any threat
if their prey has /any/ intercept. I don't think that a strategy
that can torporize (no matter how effectively) such opponents
is `too powerful'.



Any advantage this may give you would (mostly) be offset by allowing
you to take a blood off in the first turn, when the Blood Doll card
is played.

Consider this example: a capacity 7 vampire has 5 blood on it.
You have Hunting Ground out. You play Blood Doll on it. You
have two choices (among others):

1. refrain from taking a blood off this turn; put HG blood and
take it off every turn hereafter. Result: vampire always
has 5 blood on it.

2. take blood off this turn; put HG blood and take it off every
turn hereafter. Result: vampire always has 4 blood on it,
but you have one more pool than 1. above.

Most players would choose option 2, for 1 more pool. (Pool is `usually'
more important than blood on vampire.)

Now consider your case, where a capacity 5 vampire has 5 blood
on it. HG is out, and Blood Doll is played.

Under current rulings, the result is exactly the same as 2. above.
Option 1 is not availiable, because you cannot put HG blood on
a full vampire.

If Blood Doll becomes an Untap phase effect, the result would be
exactly the same as 1. above. Option 2. is no longer availiable,
because under this ruling you cannot take a blood off in the
first turn.

Thus, making Blood Doll an Untap Phase effect doesn't give any
significant advantage, unless someone believes that result 1.
is much better than result 2.

Sorry about using you folks for an object lesson, but that is exactly the
point I'm making (elsewhere) about the untap cards. Untapped minions able
to act or block are a fundamental resource in the game, and any card that
allows cheap or free untaps will cause a big problem by allowing a nearly
unlimited resource (cards) to replace a tightly restricted one (available
vampires). As long as the untaps remain so cheap, combat ends and untap
will be a nearly unbeatable strategy.

P.S. Fast reaction is one of the counters for these strategies, but you
only get one round of pounding, and Tremere have a hard time doing enough
damage the first round to make it count.
